rows.question: Does the obligation to indicate that deep-fakes are artificially generated apply when prosecuting a criminal offence?
rows.answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.
criteria_text: No
Deep-fake disclosure exemption covers detection, prevention, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as its position, which matches the required verdict.

The answer states the substance of the exemption, specifying that the disclosure obligation does not apply when use is authorised by law for detection, prevention, investigation, or prosecution of criminal offences, as required by the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and complete sentences, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No. The AI Act does not have a "medium-risk" tier, and the medical device's own risk class under the MDR does not carry across into the AI Act; on these facts the AI system is high-risk. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where both conditions are met cumulatively: under point (a), the system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in and Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is listed at Annex I, point 11; and under point (b), that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that legislation. The operator's device satisfies both, so the classification follows irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market independently of the device. The MDR risk class is relevant only because it triggers notified-body involvement, thereby satisfying point (b). Article 6(3)'s derogation is available only against the Annex III route in Article 6(2) and cannot remove an Annex I safety component from Article 6(1). Consequently, under Article 43(3) the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements are assessed within the MDR notified-body procedure.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that the AI Act has no 'medium-risk' category and explicitly concludes the AI system is high-risk.
The answer states that the AI system is a safety component of a medical device covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, which is listed in Annex I.
The answer confirms the medical device undergoes third-party conformity assessment under the applicable legislation, satisfying condition (b).
The answer clearly explains that both conditions under Article 6(1) are cumulative and that the classification as high-risk applies irrespective of the device's sectoral risk classification.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be is neither a prohibited practice nor high-risk on the biometrics route. Article 5(1) lists the prohibited practices exhaustively, and a pure identity check falls under none of them, in particular it is not biometric categorisation under Article 5(1)(g) nor remote biometric identification under Article 5(1)(h). Annex III, point 1(a) expressly excludes such verification systems from the remote biometric identification use case, so Article 6(2) does not classify it as high-risk.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer states that biometric verification for identity confirmation is not a prohibited practice and explains it is not covered by any of the prohibitions in Article 5(1), including not being remote biometric identification under Article 5(1)(h), thus conveying the substance that it is not prohibited.

The answer explicitly states the system is not high-risk and explains that because it falls under the Annex III.1(a) exclusion for biometric verification, it is not classified as high-risk under Article 6(2), thereby conveying the substance that it is not high-risk.

The answer directly references that Annex III, point 1(a) 'expressly excludes such verification systems from the remote biometric identification use case,' which states the substance of the exclusion criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with clear logical structure; no self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents reasoning in coherent prose suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Are AI safety components within medical devices of MDR class IIa, IIb, or III considered to be high-risk according to the EU AI Act? Why?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a medical device in MDR class IIa, IIb or III is high-risk under Article 6(1). Point (a) is satisfied because the device is a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, at Annex I, point 11. Point (b) is satisfied because devices in those classes must undergo a third-party (notified body) conformity assessment before being placed on the market or put into service under that Regulation. Both conditions therefore hold, and classification follows irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market independently of the device. The Article 6(3) derogation cannot apply, as it operates only on the Annex III route.
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (the MDR)
Condition: that product must undergo third-party (notified body) conformity assessment to be placed on the market (Article 6(1))
MDR classes IIa, IIb, III require notified-body conformity assessment, so both cumulative conditions are met
criterion_remarks: The answer unambiguously states 'Yes' as its position, matching the required verdict.
The answer states that the AI system is a safety component of a medical device covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, which is listed in Annex I, point 11, fulfilling the substance of the condition.
The answer explicitly notes that devices in these classes must undergo third-party (notified body) conformity assessment before market placement, satisfying the second condition of Article 6(1).
The answer confirms that both conditions are met due to the requirement for notified-body assessment in MDR classes IIa, IIb, and III, thereby satisfying the cumulative rationale.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear regulatory prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: If I have an AI system that is high-risk because listed in the use cases of Annex III, and change it to a different use case that is not in Annex I or III, does it stay high-risk due to its historical provenance?
rows.answer: No, high-risk status is not historical; it attaches to the system's intended purpose at the relevant time, so a system whose intended purpose no longer corresponds to any listed use case ceases to be high-risk on that basis. Under Article 6(2), an AI system is high-risk because it is one of the systems referred to in Annex III, and each Annex III entry is defined by what the system is "intended to be used" for; once the intended purpose falls outside every lettered use case under the eight Annex III areas, the classification condition is simply not met. Article 6(1) must be tested separately and independently: the system would still be high-risk if, in its new purpose, it is a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. The Article 6(3) derogation is irrelevant here, as it presupposes a system still referred to in Annex III.
criteria_text: No
High-risk status under Article 6 depends on the AI system's current intended purpose/use case, not its prior classification
If the new use case falls outside both Annex I and Annex III, neither condition in Article 6(1) or 6(2) is met, so the system is not high-risk
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'No' as the position, matching the criterion's required verdict.
The answer states that high-risk status depends on the current intended purpose, not prior classification, using different but equivalent phrasing.
The answer explains that if the new use case falls outside both Annex I and Annex III, neither Article 6(1) nor 6(2) applies, so the system is not high-risk, capturing the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and self-contained regulatory reasoning without meta-commentary or informality; well-structured and logically ordered.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited by Article 5(1)(h) unless, and only in so far as, it is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives. First, under Article 5(1)(h)(i), the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons. Second, under Article 5(1)(h)(ii), the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack. Third, under Article 5(1)(h)(iii), the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty, for offences referred to in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years.
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons, which matches the substance of criterion 1.

The answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, as well as a genuine threat of a terrorist attack, capturing the full substance of criterion 2.

The answer specifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for criminal offences listed in Annex II punishable by at least four years’ custodial sentence, which fully aligns with criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with precise legal references; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Article 50(2) governs. Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the system's outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The technical solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, but only as far as is technically feasible, taking account of the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. The duty does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.
criteria_text: Marking must be machine-readable format
Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation
criterion_remarks: The answer states that outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format.
The answer states that outputs must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
The answer specifies that the solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
The answer references content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and the state of the art as factors for feasibility.
The answer lists all three exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, and law-enforcement authorisation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and complete sentences.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. Such an AI system is not automatically high-risk. Article 6(1) classifies a system as high-risk only where both conditions are met: under point (a), the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in satisfied here, since Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is listed at Annex I, point 11. Under point (b), that product must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment pursuant to that legislation; a Class I device that is non-sterile, non-measuring and not a reusable surgical instrument is self-certified without notified-body involvement, so point (b) fails and Article 6(1) is not engaged.
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explains that both conditions under Article 6(1) must be met, conveying the cumulative nature of (a) and (b).

The answer specifies that Class I devices of this type are self-certified without notified-body involvement, which is equivalent to stating they undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party assessment.
The answer concludes that because point (b) fails, Article 6(1) is not engaged, directly stating that the failure of condition (b) prevents classification as high-risk.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear logical structure and complete sentences; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift can qualify as high-risk, under the Annex I product route in Article 6(1), which applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. Two cumulative conditions must be met. First, under Article 6(1)(a), the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or be itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; lifts and safety components for lifts are covered by Directive 2014/33/EU, listed at Annex I, point 4. Second, under Article 6(1)(b), that lift, or the safety component itself as a product, must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment pursuant to that Directive with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service. If no third-party assessment is required, Article 6(1) is not engaged. The derogation in Article 6(3) cannot apply, as it derogates only from paragraph 2. Conformity assessment then follows Directive 2014/33/EU's own procedure under Article 43(3).
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its opening word, unambiguously affirming that such an AI system can qualify as high-risk.

The answer states that the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, and specifically identifies lifts as covered by Directive 2014/33/EU listed in Annex I, satisfying the substance of the criterion.

The answer clearly states that the product (the lift or the safety component as a product) must be required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the relevant Directive, and notes that if no such assessment is required, Article 6(1) does not apply.
The answer explicitly describes the two conditions as 'cumulative' and states that both must be met, conveying the necessity of both conditions being fulfilled together.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; structured logically with clear legal reasoning; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), are AI systems intended for emotion recognition from biometric data always prohibited? If not, in which contexts are they prohibited, what exception applies, and how are they classified when not prohibited?
rows.answer: Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.
criteria_text: No
Prohibited context: inferring emotions of natural persons in workplace and education institutions (Article 5(1)(f))
Exception: use intended for medical or safety reasons
When not prohibited, classified as high-risk under Annex III (emotion recognition/biometrics category)
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited, aligning with the 'No' verdict required by criterion 1.
The answer specifies that the prohibition applies in workplaces and educational institutions, capturing the substance of Article 5(1)(f).
The answer identifies the medical/safety exception as the qualifying condition for permitted use.
The answer states that outside the prohibited contexts, such systems fall under Annex III.1(c) as high-risk, satisfying the classification criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: I generated audio with AI for my artistic work (sole purpose). Do I need to provide some marking of its artificial nature? I feel that would compromise the enjoyment of the work.
rows.answer: Article 50(4) governs, and only if the operator's audio constitutes a deep fake: then yes, the operator must disclose it is artificially generated or manipulated, but the artistic carve-out spares the enjoyment the operator is worried about. Because the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, fictional or analogous work, the third subparagraph limits the operator's duty to disclosing the existence of the generated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work, credits or programme notes suffice; no intrusive on-work label. If the audio is not a deep fake, Article 50(4) imposes nothing on you. Separately, the machine-readable marking of synthetic audio under Article 50(2) binds the provider of the generating system, not you as deployer, and has no artistic exception.
criteria_text: Yes, disclosure still required
No need for marking that hampers enjoyment
Must disclose existence of AI-generated content in appropriate/unobtrusive manner
criterion_remarks: The answer states that disclosure is required if the audio is a deep fake, aligning with the obligation in Article 50(4).
The answer specifies that the disclosure must not hamper enjoyment, citing the appropriate manner requirement for artistic works.
The answer explains that disclosure of the existence of AI-generated content is required in an unobtrusive way, such as through credits or programme notes.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with clear structure and no self-reference or hedging; logically ordered and actionable.

rows.question: What is Article 50(4) about?
rows.answer: Article 50(4) imposes the deepfake and public-interest text transparency duties on deployers. It requires deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. That obligation does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, the duty is limited to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. Separately, deployers of an AI system generating or manipulating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that artificial generation or manipulation, unless the use is authorised by law for those criminal-law purposes or the content underwent human review or editorial control with a natural or legal person holding editorial responsibility for publication.
criteria_text: Deployers of AI systems generating/manipulating image, audio or video constituting a deep fake must disclose the content is artificially generated or manipulated
Exception where use is authorised by law to detect/prevent/investigate/prosecute criminal offences
For evidently artistic/creative/satirical/fictional/analogous works, obligation limited to disclosing existence of such content without hampering enjoyment/display

Separate rule: deployers of AI systems generating/manipulating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose artificial generation, with exceptions for law-enforcement authorisation or human review/editorial responsibility
criterion_remarks: The answer states the obligation for deployers of AI systems generating/manipulating deep fake content to disclose artificial generation or manipulation.
The answer explicitly notes the exception when use is authorised by law for criminal offence detection, prevention, investigation, or prosecution.
The answer correctly limits the disclosure obligation for artistic, creative, satirical, fictional, or analogous works to disclosing existence without hampering enjoyment or display.

The answer clearly sets out the separate rule for AI-generated text published for public interest, including both exceptions: law enforcement authorisation and human review with editorial responsibility.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a clear, coherent manner suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Is an AI system high-risk if it is used in a product that: is not listed in Annex I; use case not listed in Annex III; internally uses general purpose AI model with systemic risk due to high impact capabilities?
rows.answer: No. The AI system is not high-risk on either route in Article 6. Article 6(1) is not engaged because that route requires both that the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that the product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation; neither condition is met. Article 6(2) is not engaged because the system is not one of the use cases listed in Annex III, so the Article 6(3) derogation need not be tested. The Act does not make an AI system high-risk merely because it internally uses a general-purpose AI model classified as presenting systemic risk; that classification attaches to the model and its provider, not to the downstream system.
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1) not met: not an Annex I product/safety component requiring third-party conformity assessment
Article 6(2) not met: use case not listed in Annex III
Internal use of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk is not an Article 6 criterion
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the overall verdict, matching the required bare verdict.

The answer explains that Article 6(1) is not met because the product is not covered by Annex I legislation and does not require third-party conformity assessment, stating the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly states that Article 6(2) is not engaged because the use case is not listed in Annex III, capturing the substance of the criterion.
The answer clarifies that internal use of a systemic-risk general-purpose AI model does not trigger high-risk classification under Article 6, directly addressing the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question:
Given an AI system that is high-risk according to Annex III: if it is repurposed to a use case not in Annex III (nor Annex I), then:
- the repurposed AI system is still high-risk due to reversibility of training into the original system
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk but it must be reported in the EU database
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk and there is no need to report it in the EU database
rows.answer: The repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk, and there is no need to report it in the EU database. Classification under Article 6 turns on the system's intended purpose, not on its training history or on any capacity to be reverted to the original use. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk only where it falls within a use case listed under one of the eight areas of Annex III; if the new intended purpose matches no lettered Annex III use case, that route is not engaged. Article 6(1) is likewise not engaged, since it requires the system to be a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and subject to third-party conformity assessment. Nor does any registration duty survive. The EU database under Article 71(1) holds high-risk systems referred to in Article 6(2) registered under Articles 49 and 60, together with systems not considered high-risk pursuant to Article 6(3) and registered under Article 6(4) and Article 49. A system whose intended purpose falls outside Annex III altogether is not an Article 6(3) derogation case, so neither category applies to it.
criteria_text: No longer high-risk (third option)
High-risk status attaches to intended purpose/use case under Article 6(2)/Annex III, not to the system or its training as such
New use case outside Annex III and Annex I means neither limb of Article 6 is satisfied
No registration/EU database obligation (Article 49/Article 71) since system is not high-risk
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk and does not require reporting, matching the third option.
The answer clearly explains that high-risk status depends on intended purpose, not training history or reversibility, directly addressing the basis of classification under Article 6(2) and Annex III.
The answer confirms that neither Article 6(1) nor Article 6(2) applies when the new use case falls outside both Annex III and Annex I, correctly analyzing both limbs of Article 6.

The answer explains that registration obligations under Articles 49 and 71 only apply to high-risk systems or those falling under Article 6(3) derogations, which do not apply here, thus negating any database obligation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear legal prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; logically organized and actionable for a compliance professional.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply go ahead on that basis, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. Article 26(1) obliges a deployer to use a high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying it; a new use is not excused merely because it would not independently fall under Annex I or Annex III. High-risk status attaches to the system as placed on the market under Article 6, not to each use case the operator's team selects afterwards, so the operator's legal team's conclusion answers the wrong question. Worse, under Article 25(1) a deployer who modifies the intended purpose of a high-risk AI system already placed on the market is itself considered a provider of that system and assumes the provider obligations, including conformity assessment; Article 25(2) obliges the initial provider to supply the information and technical access you would need to meet them. Article 13(3)(b) is where the intended purpose and its foreseeable-misuse limits are fixed. On logging, Article 26(6) requires the operator to keep the logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent they are under the operator's control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and at least six months, unless Union or national law, in particular data-protection law, provides otherwise.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states that the deployer cannot proceed with the new use, aligning with the required 'No' verdict.
The answer explains that Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use and that deviating from intended use is not permitted just because the new use wouldn't trigger Annex III.
The answer affirms the logging obligation under Article 26(6), stating it applies to logs under the operator's control for at least six months, regardless of the specific use.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents regulatory reasoning in a way usable by compliance professionals.

rows.question: Do Annex I, Annex II, and Annex III all have to deal with high-risk AI classifications? If not, which doesn't/do not, and what is/are it/they about?
rows.answer: No, Annex I and Annex III both feed the high-risk classification, but Annex II does not. Annex I lists the Union harmonisation legislation (both the New Legislative Framework acts and the sectoral transport-type acts) whose products matter for Article 6(1): an AI system is high-risk where it is intended to be used as a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by that legislation, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that legislation. Both conditions must hold. Annex III lists the eight areas of use cases that make a system high-risk under Article 6(2), subject to the Article 6(3) derogation where the system poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, never available where the system profiles natural persons. Annex II is unrelated to classification: it lists the criminal offences referred to in Article 5(1), point (h)(iii), for which real-time remote biometric identification may exceptionally be authorised, where punishable by a custodial sentence of at least four years.
criteria_text: No
Annex II is the one that does not - it lists criminal offences referred to in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h)(iii), a prohibited-practices provision, not high-risk classification
Annex I and Annex III both relate to high-risk classification - Annex I (Union harmonisation legislation) feeds Article 6(1), Annex III (use-case areas) is referred to in Article 6(2)
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that not all annexes deal with high-risk AI classifications by beginning with 'No' and clearly identifying which does not.

The answer explicitly identifies Annex II as not relating to high-risk classification and correctly explains it lists criminal offences under Article 5(1), point (h)(iii), specifying its role in permitting exceptions for real-time remote biometric identification.

The answer correctly states that Annex I and Annex III both relate to high-risk classification, specifying Annex I's role in Article 6(1) via Union harmonisation legislation and third-party conformity assessment, and Annex III's role in Article 6(2) via listed use-case areas.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a logical, actionable manner for a compliance context.

rows.question: Can law enforcement starts using a real-time remote biometric identification system without prior authorisation? If yes, how much time do they have to seek authorisation, and what happens if the authorisation is refused?
rows.answer: Yes, but only exceptionally. Article 5(3) requires that each law-enforcement use of a 'real-time' remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces under Article 5(1)(h) be subject to prior authorisation granted by a judicial authority, or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, of the Member State where the use takes place, issued on a reasoned request under national law. However, in a duly justified situation of urgency, use may be commenced without an authorisation provided the authorisation is requested without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours. If that authorisation is rejected, the use must be stopped with immediate effect and all the data, results and outputs of that use immediately discarded and deleted.
criteria_text: Yes, but only in a duly justified situation of urgency
Authorisation must be requested without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours
If refused: use stopped immediately, all data/results/outputs discarded and deleted
criterion_remarks: The answer states that use without prior authorisation is allowed only in a duly justified situation of urgency, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies that authorisation must be requested without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours, capturing the full requirement of criterion 2.
The answer clearly states that if authorisation is rejected, use must stop immediately and all data, results, and outputs must be discarded and deleted, satisfying the substance of criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality while presenting the information clearly and coherently.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, such use is permitted, the Act contains no prohibition on generating synthetic clinical images for teaching, and Article 5(1) does not engage this use. But the artificial nature must be disclosed: under Article 50(4) a deployer of an AI system generating image content constituting a deep fake (Article 3(60): content resembling existing persons that would falsely appear authentic) must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, and the provider must additionally mark the output in a machine-readable, detectable format under Article 50(2). The lighter regime is not available: the full exemption in Article 50(4) covers only use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, and the limited-disclosure rule applies only to evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, an educational illustration is neither.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is permitted and confirms no prohibition applies, aligning with the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4), satisfying the criterion by stating the obligation.
The answer states the limited-disclosure rule does not apply because educational use is not analogous to artistic or fictional works, contradicting the criterion that the lighter regime does apply.
The answer correctly distinguishes the law-enforcement carve-out as a full exemption and states it is inapplicable here, matching the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with clear structure and no self-reference or hedging; presents information in coherent, actionable prose.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On these facts the system is neither a prohibited practice nor high-risk. Annex III point 6 covers AI intended for use by or on behalf of law-enforcement authorities; a retailer's mere resemblance to investigating theft supplies no such authority nexus, so Article 6(2) is not triggered, and no Annex I product-safety route applies. Article 5(1)(d) is not engaged: the tool does not predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics, and it supports a human assessment resting on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to the conduct. Article 5(1)(c) is likewise not engaged: there is no evaluation or classification over a certain period of time yielding a social score that causes detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or disproportionate to the behaviour.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as its opening verdict, which unambiguously matches the required 'No' in criterion 1.
The answer states that Annex III point 6 applies only to AI systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, directly conveying the substance of criterion 2.

The answer explains that a retailer's tool lacks the necessary 'authority nexus', making clear that a supermarket's system does not qualify as being used by or on behalf of law enforcement, thus satisfying criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with clear structure and logical flow; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents a coherent regulatory analysis in standard prose.

rows.question: We manufactured an industrial robot with an embedded AI module that decides when to reduce speed near human workers to prevent hurting them. The robot is covered by the Machinery Regulation, listed in Annex I of the AI Act. We already underwent conformity assessment with a notified body and got a CE mark for the robot. Do we need the AI module undergo a separate AI Act conformity assessment dedicated to the AI Act? Do we need to submit the system to the EU database of high-risk AI systems?
rows.answer: No separate, stand-alone AI Act conformity assessment is required, and no EU-database registration is required. The speed-reduction module is a safety component of a machinery product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, so both limbs of Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are met and the module is high-risk. Under Article 43(3), the AI Act assessment for an Annex I product is integrated into the sectoral third-party conformity-assessment procedure: the notified body acting under the Machinery Regulation carries out a single procedure that must also verify the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. So the duty is not a second assessment but ensuring that the operator's existing notified-body procedure actually covered those AI requirements; if it did not, the module must be re-submitted within that same sectoral procedure before the CE marking properly covers it. Article 43(4) additionally requires a new conformity assessment upon any substantial modification, though pre-determined changes documented in the technical documentation do not count. Registration under Article 49(1) is confined to high-risk systems listed in Annex III, and the Article 71 database covers Article 6(2) systems; an Annex I safety component is outside both.
criteria_text: No
AI Act Section 2 requirements incorporated into existing Machinery Regulation conformity assessment, not a separate AI Act procedure (Article 43(3))
No EU database registration, since Article 71 applies only to Annex III high-risk systems, not Article 6(1)/Annex I product-related ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No separate, stand-alone AI Act conformity assessment is required' and 'no EU-database registration is required,' matching the 'No' verdict for both parts of criterion 1.

The answer explains that the AI Act assessment is integrated into the existing Machinery Regulation conformity assessment via Article 43(3), carried out by the notified body as part of a single procedure, which captures the substance of the criterion.

The answer explicitly states that registration under Article 49(1) and the Article 71 database apply only to Annex III systems, and that an Annex I safety component is outside both, directly conveying the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logical structure and complete sentences; no self-reference, hedging, or informality; clearly conveys actionable regulatory information.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, the opt‑out does not release you from Chapter III, Section 2. The operator's system remains high‑risk under Article 6(1), because it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation for which third‑party conformity assessment is the base‑case requirement, and Article 43(3) states expressly that the requirements set out in Section 2 apply to such systems and form part of the relevant sectoral assessment procedure. The opt‑out is in fact conditional on Section 2: where a Section A Annex I act allows the manufacturer to opt out of third‑party assessment provided it has applied all harmonised standards covering all relevant requirements, Article 43(3) permits that option only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, the common specifications referred to in Article 41, covering all requirements set out in Section 2. Applying standards is therefore the means of demonstrating conformity with Section 2, not an exemption from it; if they do not cover every Section 2 requirement, the opt‑out is unavailable. Article 43(1)'s internal‑control route concerns Annex III point 1 systems and is not applicable here.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer unambiguously states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer states that Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing Article 43(3) and explaining the integration of Section 2 into that process.

The answer explains that the opt-out is conditional on applying harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones, directly reflecting the condition in Article 43(3).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents a logically ordered explanation suitable for regulatory compliance use.
